newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Two Russian journalists freed in Chechnya - Tass.
newsitem.headline: Two Russian journalists freed in Chechnya - Tass.

text.p: Two Russian journalists held hostage in Chechnya were freed on Sunday on the eve of tough talks between President Boris Yeltsin and Chechen leader Aslan Maskhadov, Itar-Tass news agency said.

The journalists from the private VID television channel, seized in the breakaway region's capital Grozny on June 11, were freed after a joint operation by Russian and Chechen security forces, Tass quoted an official in Russia's Security Council as saying. The journalists were due in Moscow later on Sunday.
Officials in Grozny declined to comment on the report.
The news came two days after security forces in Grozny rescued an ethnic Chechen hostage. A policeman was killed in that operation.
Yeltsin is expected to press Maskhadov during Monday's talks in the Kremlin to do more to help free the many Russian and foreign hostages seized in Chechnya by gunmen seeking ransoms.
Maskhadov, who has said hostage takers face the death penalty or tough prison sentences, convened a meeting of his security chiefs on Sunday to discuss the hostage issue, Interfax news agency said.
Two Britons, five French people, a German, a Slovak and a Yugoslav are among those currently missing in Chechnya.
In Moscow Russian and Chechen negotiators continued to prepare the ground for Maskhadov's talks with Yeltsin, which are also expected to touch on the thorny issue of Chechnya's status.

Maskhadov has made clear he will not back off from his demand that Moscow recognise his tiny Caucasus region as a sovereign state. On Saturday he said he wanted Russia and Chechnya to establish full-fledged diplomatic relations.

The Kremlin, whose troops were humiliated by Maskhadov's separatist guerrillas during a bloody 21-month conflict that ended last August, says Chechnya must stay within the Russian Federation, although with wide autonomy.
Ekho Moskvy radio on Sunday quoted an unnamed source in Russia's Security Council as saying Chechnya's demand for full-fledged diplomatic ties were unacceptable.
"Russia will do everything to prevent this from happening," he was quoted as saying.

Interfax said the Security Council's secretary, Ivan Rybkin, and Chechen First Deputy Prime Minister Movladi Udugov had signed a protocol allowing family members of people missing in Chechnya to play a more active role in trying to locate them.
Rybkin has said the number of people still missing, including people taken captive during the war, totals 1,407.
